bodyHtml:
Top spots for location-independent professionals

December 31, 2017
Freelancer tips | Globalisation | Lifestyle

Are you weighing up where to live as a location-independent professional, or where to base yourself as a freelance translator? More people now work remotely for UK clients while living abroad, and the choice of base affects your visa, your tax position and your working day.

This article covers the checks to make before you leave the UK, the features worth looking for and a shortlist of places that suit remote workers.

Checks to make before you leave the UK

The destination matters less than the paperwork behind it. Settle these points first.

Your UK tax residence

Whether you pay UK tax on your worldwide income depends on the Statutory Residence Test, which counts the days you spend in the UK in a tax year running from 6 April to 5 April. GOV.UK explains that you are generally non-resident if you spend fewer than 16 days in the UK, or fewer than 46 days if you were not UK resident in the three previous tax years.

There is also an overseas work test for people who work full-time abroad. Read the HMRC guidance, or speak to an accountant, before you assume you have left the UK system.

The right visa

A tourist stamp is not a licence to work. Several countries now run visas for remote workers, including Spain, Portugal, Thailand, Malaysia and Colombia, and each sets its own income, insurance and documentation rules.

Most of these visas require your income to come from outside the country. Thailand's Destination Thailand Visa, for example, is valid for five years with stays of up to 180 days per entry, and the Royal Thai Embassy asks for evidence of at least 500,000 THB in funds. Always check the embassy or immigration authority's own page, because requirements change.

Travel advice and insurance

The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) publishes travel advice for every country, covering safety, entry rules and health. Check it before you book, and arrange insurance that covers remote work and medical treatment where you will be living.

What to look for in a base

Everybody pictures a different life. You might want cobbled streets and fresh bread in a small town, a surf beach after work or mountain trails at the weekend.

Whatever you choose, most remote workers need the same practical things:

  • reliable fibre or mobile internet, with a backup connection
  • a time zone that overlaps with your clients' working hours
  • a cost of living that fits your income
  • co-working spaces or cafés where you can meet other remote workers
  • straightforward healthcare, banking and visa renewals

Home comforts count too. If you are moving abroad from Britain, you may find our post on the British food that expats miss a useful reminder of what to pack.

Places that suit remote professionals

Lisbon and Portugal

Portugal offers a D8 visa for remote workers, and Lisbon has co-working spaces and an international freelance community. Mainland Portugal shares the UK's time zone, which helps if your clients are in Britain.

Valencia and Spain

Spain created a visa for international teleworkers under its Startup Act, Law 28/2022. Valencia and other coastal cities give you the sea and good transport links, with only a one-hour time difference from the UK.

Medellín, Colombia

Dubbed the City of Eternal Spring for its mild climate, Medellín has co-working spaces, a busy social scene and a visa category for digital nomads. The visa requires income from abroad and does not allow you to work for Colombian employers.

Chiang Mai, Thailand

Chiang Mai is a long-standing favourite with remote workers. The city sits among mountains and has co-working spaces and cafés aimed at people working online.

Penang, Malaysia

Penang is known for its food and its mix of cultures. Malaysia's DE Rantau programme issues a pass to remote workers, and income rules differ for technology and non-technology roles, so check the current rules.

Keeping your work running from abroad

Your clients should not notice that you have moved. Agree working hours and response times in advance, and tell them which time zone you are in.

Check how you will invoice and be paid, particularly if your clients pay in sterling and your costs are in another currency. If you handle confidential documents, agree data protection terms with your clients and use a secure connection rather than public Wi-Fi.

If you are a translator or interpreter

Working remotely has a particular advantage for linguists: you can live where your language is spoken. A translator who lives in Spain hears current Spanish every day, which keeps idiom, register and cultural references fresh.

BeTranslated works with professional translators in many countries. If your clients need document translation or a translated website, our native translators work into their mother tongue.

Planning a move for your business instead? Request a free, no-obligation quote and tell us which languages you need.

Frequently asked questions

Do I still pay UK tax if I work abroad?

It depends on the Statutory Residence Test, which looks at how many days you spend in the UK and your ties to it. You may stay UK resident if you spend 183 days or more in the UK in a tax year. Check HMRC guidance or ask an accountant.

Can I work on a tourist visa abroad?

Often not. Many countries restrict work on a tourist stay, even remote work for foreign clients. A remote work or digital nomad visa gives you a clear legal basis.

Which countries offer visas for remote workers?

Spain, Portugal, Thailand, Malaysia and Colombia all run schemes for remote workers. Each has its own income and documentation rules, so use the official government or embassy page for the latest requirements.

What should I check about internet and time zones?

Test the connection before you commit, ask about backup options and check how many working hours you share with your clients. A good base for a UK-facing role is usually within a few hours of London time.

Can a freelance translator work from any country?

Yes, provided you meet visa and tax rules, secure data and hold the right equipment. Many translators choose to live in a country where their working language is spoken.
